content: 1. Isoniazid is an oral antitubercular and antibacterial agent approved by the FDA for treating all forms of tuberculosis caused by susceptible organisms. 2. The drug carries a Black Box Warning, indicating significant risks associated with its use. 3. Common adverse reactions to isoniazid include elevated liver enzymes, neuropathy, and neurotoxicity. 4. For adults with active pulmonary tuberculosis caused by drug-susceptible organisms, treatment involves an initial phase of two months with a four-drug combination (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol), followed by a continuation phase lasting 4 to 7 months with isoniazid and either rifampin or rifapentine. 5. In HIV-infected patients with active tuberculosis, the recommended dose of isoniazid is 5 mg/kg daily (maximum 300 mg per dose) or 15 mg/kg two to three times weekly (maximum 900 mg per dose) in combination with other TB medications. Twice-weekly dosing is not recommended for HIV patients with CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³. 6. For HIV-infected individuals with latent tuberculosis, the recommended dose of isoniazid is 300 mg orally daily or 900 mg orally twice weekly, with pyridoxine (50 mg daily) administered concurrently to reduce the risk of peripheral neuropathy. The prophylaxis duration is nine months. 7. An alternative regimen for HIV-infected, nonpregnant adults not on antiretroviral therapy is a 12-week course of isoniazid (15 mg/kg, maximum 900 mg) plus rifapentine, administered once weekly under directly observed therapy. 8. For patients with inactive tuberculosis, the preferred regimen is 5 mg/kg (maximum 300 mg) orally daily for nine months or 15 mg/kg (maximum 900 mg) orally twice weekly for nine months under directly observed therapy. 9. Pediatric dosing for active TB includes isoniazid 10–15 mg/kg daily (maximum 300 mg/day) in combination with rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for eight weeks, followed by a continuation phase of isoniazid and rifampin. 10. For children with latent TB, the preferred regimen is isoniazid 10–20 mg/kg (maximum 300 mg) orally daily for nine months or 20–40 mg/kg (maximum 900 mg) orally twice weekly under directly observed therapy. 11. Isoniazid is contraindicated in patients with severe hypersensitivity reactions, drug-induced hepatitis, previous isoniazid-associated hepatic injury, or acute liver disease of any etiology. 12. The drug should be used cautiously in individuals with chronic liver disease, severe renal dysfunction, daily alcohol use, pregnancy, or conditions predisposing to neuropathy. 13. Adverse effects include peripheral neuropathy (dose-related, more common in malnourished individuals or those predisposed to neuritis), neurotoxic effects (e.g., convulsions, toxic encephalopathy, optic neuritis), and hepatic reactions (elevated transaminases, jaundice, and potentially fatal hepatitis). 14. Isoniazid should not be administered with food, as its bioavailability is significantly reduced. Foods containing tyramine (e.g., cheese, red wine) or histamine (e.g., tuna, skipjack) should be avoided due to potential interactions. 15. Drug interactions include increased serum levels of carbamazepine, phenytoin, and valproate when co-administered with isoniazid, necessitating close monitoring and dosage adjustments. 16. Isoniazid is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA, indicating potential risks to the fetus. However, it is recommended for treating active tuberculosis during pregnancy when the benefits outweigh the risks. Preventive therapy is generally deferred until after delivery. 17. Small amounts of isoniazid in breast milk are not toxic to nursing infants, and breastfeeding should not be discouraged. However, these levels are insufficient for prophylaxis or therapy in the infant. 18. There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of isoniazid in geriatric, pediatric, or immunocompromised populations, nor in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 19. Physicians prescribing isoniazid should be familiar with tuberculosis treatment guidelines and perform drug susceptibility testing on initial isolates to guide therapy. 20.
